Compute CAC (Confidence-Accuracy Characteristic) Data

Source: R/cac_functions.R
make_cacdata.Rd

Computes confidence-accuracy data for lineup identifications following Mickes (2015). CAC analysis shows the relationship between confidence and accuracy for suspect identifications.

Usage

make_cacdata(
  data,
  lineup_size = 6,
  confidence_bins = NULL,
  innocent_suspect = "auto",
  base_rate = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A dataframe with the following columns:

  • target_present: Logical. TRUE if guilty suspect in lineup

  • identification: Character. "suspect", "filler", or "reject"

  • confidence: Numeric. Confidence rating

lineup_size

Integer. Number of people in lineup (default = 6)

confidence_bins

Numeric vector of bin edges for grouping confidence (e.g., c(0, 60, 80, 100) creates bins 0-60, 61-80, 81-100). If NULL, uses individual confidence levels.

innocent_suspect

How innocent-suspect identifications in target-absent lineups are obtained. "designated": the lineups had a designated innocent suspect, so target-absent "suspect" rows are counted directly, and zero such rows means a false-ID rate of zero. "estimated": there was no designated innocent suspect, so the innocent-suspect count is estimated as filler IDs divided by lineup_size. "auto" (the default) chooses "designated" when any target-absent row is a suspect ID or the data have a non-missing suspect_pos column, and "estimated" otherwise, with a message.

base_rate

Prior probability that the suspect is guilty, used to compute accuracy from rates rather than counts. NULL (default) keeps the count definition of Mickes (2015). A number strictly between 0 and 1 gives \(\pi HR(c) / (\pi HR(c) + (1 - \pi) FAR(c))\); see Details.

Value

A list containing:

  • cac_data: Dataframe with confidence levels and accuracy

  • overall_accuracy: Overall accuracy across all suspect IDs

  • n_total_suspect_ids: Correct plus incorrect suspect IDs

  • base_rate: The base rate used, or NULL for count-based accuracy

  • n_target_present, n_target_absent: Sample sizes of the two arms

Details

CAC analysis computes, for each confidence level: $$Accuracy = \frac{Correct Suspect IDs}{Correct Suspect IDs + Incorrect Suspect IDs}$$

Explicit target-absent suspect IDs are used when present. Otherwise, target-absent filler IDs are divided by lineup size to estimate incorrect suspect IDs. The two estimators are never added together.

The count ratio equals the probability of guilt given a suspect ID only when the target-present and target-absent samples are the same size, which Mickes (2015) assumes; she notes that unequal base rates make the calculation more complicated. With unequal samples the count-based accuracy shifts with the TP:TA split even when hit and false-ID rates are unchanged, and the function says so in a message. Setting base_rate computes accuracy from the hit rate HR(c) = correct IDs / n(TP) and the false-ID rate FAR(c) = incorrect IDs / n(TA) at the stated prior, so that base_rate = 0.5 gives the balanced-design value whatever the sample sizes. Its standard error is then a delta-method approximation from the two independent binomial rates; the count-based standard error is binomial over the bin's suspect IDs.

According to Mickes (2015), CAC analysis is most relevant for triers of fact (judges/jurors) evaluating estimator variables (e.g., exposure duration, retention interval). It shows how trustworthy an ID is at different confidence levels.

References

Mickes, L. (2015). Receiver operating characteristic analysis and confidence-accuracy characteristic analysis in investigations of system variables and estimator variables that affect eyewitness memory. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 4(2), 93-102.

Juslin, P., Olsson, N., & Winman, A. (1996). Calibration and diagnosticity of confidence in eyewitness identification: Comments on what can be inferred from the low confidence-accuracy correlation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 22(5), 1304-1316.

Examples

data(lineup_example)
cac <- make_cacdata(lineup_example, confidence_bins = c(0, 60, 80, 100))
cac$cac_data
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   confidence n_correct n_incorrect n_total accuracy     se
#>   <chr>          <int>       <int>   <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 [0,60]           233          72     305    0.764 0.0243
#> 2 (60,80]           82          12      94    0.872 0.0344
#> 3 (80,100]         100           4     104    0.962 0.0189
